fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I have a complicated relationship with this question, because SWE-bench came out of my group and I'm proud of it, but I also think it represents a fairly narrow slice of what we actually care about.

The thing SWE-bench does well is that it's grounded in real work. Real GitHub issues, real repositories, real tests that decide whether you fixed it. That was the big shift from the earlier generation of coding benchmarks, where you'd get a function signature and a docstring and fill in twenty lines. But it's still a static snapshot. The task is fully specified, the model gets one shot, and nobody is sitting on the other side of the conversation.

That's the piece I'd most like evaluations to pick up. In practice, almost no task arrives fully specified. A software engineer gets a vague ticket, asks a couple of questions, pokes around the codebase, realizes the request doesn't quite make sense, and goes back to the person who filed it. So I want evaluations where there's a simulated user in the loop, where the information is incomplete on purpose, and where part of what you're measuring is whether the agent knows when to ask versus when to just act. We tried to build some of that into tau-bench, where the agent has to talk to a user and follow a set of policies at the same time, and it turns out models that look great on single-turn tasks fall apart quickly when the human is a moving target.

The second thing is reliability rather than peak performance. If you run an agent eight times on the same task, does it succeed eight times, or does it succeed once and you got lucky? For deployment, the consistency number matters far more than the headline accuracy, and almost none of our benchmarks report it.

And then the last one, which is harder, is measuring the process and not just the outcome. Did the agent do something unsafe along the way? Did it burn through resources? Did it leave the codebase in a reasonable state? A fix that passes the tests but deletes half the test file to get there should not count as a win. I think we need evaluations that look at the trajectory, not just the final diff.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because we built SWE-bench and have watched it go from "models barely solve anything" to being close to saturated in a fairly short time. That's a good sign for progress, but it also shows where the next generation of evaluations needs to go.

The first direction is moving from single-shot task completion to **interaction**. In SWE-bench you hand the model a well-specified GitHub issue, and there's a test suite that tells you whether it's right. Real work almost never looks like that. A real user is vague, changes their mind halfway through, leaves out important context, or asks for something that conflicts with company policy. That's a big part of what we tried to capture with tau-bench: an agent talking to a simulated user, using tools, and following a domain policy at the same time. I think we need many more evaluations where a human, or a realistic simulation of one, is in the loop, and where knowing when to ask a clarifying question counts as part of the skill.

The second is **reliability rather than peak capability**. Most benchmarks report something like pass@1 or pass@k: can the model do this at least once? If you're deploying an agent to handle thousands of customer conversations or to touch a production codebase, what matters is whether it does the right thing every time. That's why we pushed a metric like pass^k, which asks whether the agent succeeds on all k trials of the same task. When you measure that way, the numbers drop sharply, and that gap between "can do it sometimes" and "does it consistently" is where a lot of the real deployment pain lives.

Third, **longer horizons and more open-ended outcomes**. Fixing one issue in one repo is a pretty contained unit of work. I'd like to see evaluations where an agent has to build and maintain something over days or weeks: handle evolving requirements, live with its own earlier design decisions, coordinate with other agents or people. The hard part is that you lose the clean unit-test oracle, so we'll need better ways to grade, whether that's carefully designed rubrics, hidden test suites, or model-based judges we've actually validated against human judgment.

Fourth, I think evaluations should look at **process and side effects, not just final outcomes**. An agent that passes the tests but deleted a config file along the way, or leaked some data, or violated a rule it was told to follow, shouldn't get full credit. As agents get more autonomy, measuring how they got to the answer, and whether they stayed within bounds, becomes just as important as whether they got there.

And finally, **cost and efficiency**. Two agents with the same accuracy, where one uses ten times the compute or takes ten times as long, are not equivalent in practice. Benchmarks should report that tradeoff explicitly.

There's also a meta-point: static benchmarks have a shelf life, both because of saturation and contamination. So I'm excited about evaluations that are continuously refreshed and drawn from real, ongoing workflows, so they stay tied to the actual economic and practical value we care about rather than to a fixed snapshot.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, SWE-bench has been great, and I'm obviously happy with how much the community has embraced it, but I think it also represents a paradigm that we need to move beyond. These static benchmarks — you collect a fixed set of tasks, you define a pass/fail criterion, and you report a single number — they were really useful for driving progress, but they have a few fundamental limitations that are becoming more apparent as models get deployed in the real world.

The first thing I'd like to see is a move toward measuring reliability, not just capability. Right now, most benchmarks ask: can the model solve this task at least once? But if you're actually deploying an agent, the question you care about is: will it solve this task every time, consistently? A model that succeeds 70% of the time on average but behaves unpredictably on any given instance is very different from one that reliably succeeds on a well-defined 70% of tasks. So instead of pass-at-k, we should be thinking about something more like pass-to-the-k — does the agent succeed on all k attempts? When you measure things that way, the numbers drop dramatically, and that gap is actually where a lot of the interesting work lies.

The second direction is interaction. Most benchmarks are single-shot: here's a fully specified problem, produce a solution. But real tasks don't come fully specified. A software engineer gets a vague issue report and has to ask clarifying questions, explore the codebase, run tests, revise their understanding. Real users change their minds mid-conversation, give underspecified instructions, or are themselves wrong about what they want. Evaluations need to capture that back-and-forth — which probably means simulating users, with all the messiness that entails, rather than just grading a final artifact.

Third, I think we need to evaluate consequences, not just correctness. In domains like customer service or anything with real-world side effects, an agent isn't just producing text — it's taking actions: issuing refunds, modifying databases, sending emails. The evaluation has to check whether the agent followed the policies it was given, whether it took unauthorized actions, whether the end state of the world is right. That's a much richer notion of success than matching a reference answer.

And finally, there's the contamination and saturation problem. Any static benchmark that becomes popular ends up in training data, directly or indirectly, and gets climbed within a year or two. So I think the future is more dynamic evaluation — benchmarks that refresh continuously from live sources, or procedurally generated tasks where memorization doesn't help. We need evaluation to be a living process rather than a frozen artifact.

If I had to sum it up: benchmarks got us to models that are impressively capable. What we need now is evaluations that tell us whether these systems are trustworthy enough to actually hand off real work to — and that's a much harder, and honestly more interesting, measurement problem.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, so I think SWE-bench was a really important milestone, and I don't want to take anything away from it — it did the thing a good benchmark should do, which is give the field a shared, verifiable target that actually correlates with something people care about. But I think we're starting to see the limits of that whole paradigm, and they're not limits you fix by making a harder version of the same thing.

The first issue is that almost all of these benchmarks are static and fully specified. You're handed a problem statement, there's a hidden test suite, and the question is whether you produce a patch that passes. But that's not what real work looks like. In real work the task is underspecified, the person asking you doesn't fully know what they want, and a huge part of competence is figuring out what question you're actually being asked. So one direction I'm really interested in is evaluations where the agent has to gather information — ask a clarifying question, go read the right part of the codebase, run an experiment to disambiguate between two hypotheses. And then you're measuring something much more interesting than final accuracy. You're measuring whether it knew what it didn't know.

The second thing is that we almost exclusively score outcomes and almost never score trajectories. Two agents can both get the issue resolved, and one of them did it in four tool calls and the other burned a few hundred thousand tokens, rewrote six files it shouldn't have touched, and left the repo in a state where a human has to go audit it. Those are not the same result. I think cost, number of actions, collateral damage, recoverability when things go wrong — those should be first-class metrics, not footnotes in an appendix.

And related to that: reliability. We report means on these things, and the mean is hiding the part that actually matters for deployment, which is the variance and the tail. If an agent succeeds eighty percent of the time but the twenty percent includes silently corrupting something, that's a very different product than something that's right seventy percent of the time and cleanly fails otherwise. We should be reporting distributions over repeated runs, and we should care a lot about worst-case behavior.

Then there's contamination, which I think is more corrosive than people admit. Any static benchmark has a half-life now. The moment it's useful, it's in the training data, directly or through a thousand blog posts analyzing it. So I think we need benchmarks that are living — continuously sourced from new real-world activity, or procedurally generated so you can draw fresh instances from a distribution rather than a fixed set, with held-out private components. Something closer to how we do security or forecasting, where the ground truth arrives from the future.

The last one, which is the one I personally find most compelling and the hardest to do: human-centered evaluation. The actual question for most of these systems is not "can it do the task autonomously," it's "does it make a person who's doing the task better off." Those can come apart badly. You can have a system that scores higher on autonomous benchmarks and is worse to work with, because it's confidently wrong in ways that are expensive to detect, or because the interaction overhead eats the gains. Measuring that requires studies with real people doing real work, which is slow and expensive and doesn't produce a nice number you can put on a leaderboard. But I think if we don't invest in it, we're going to keep optimizing a proxy that drifts further and further from the thing we want.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think SWE-bench was a great step, because it moved us from toy problems to real tasks with real repositories and real tests. But it has limits, and I'd want evaluations to go in a few directions from here.

First, they should be more interactive. Most benchmarks give the model a fully specified task and check one final output. Real work isn't like that. The requirements are vague, they change, and you have to ask questions, deal with a user who changes their mind, and follow rules while doing it. So I'd like evaluations that include a simulated or real human in the loop and measure how well the agent handles that back-and-forth.

Second, reliability matters more than we've been measuring. A system that solves a task 60% of the time sounds impressive, but if you run it ten times and it gives different outcomes, you can't deploy it. We should be reporting consistency across repeated attempts, not just best-case success.

Third, we need longer-horizon, more open-ended tasks that look like a day or a week of someone's job, where success isn't a single unit test passing. That means grading things like code quality, maintainability, and whether the agent made reasonable decisions along the way, not just whether the final answer is correct.

Finally, I'd want evaluations that stay fresh. Static benchmarks get saturated and contaminated quickly, so we need ones that are continually updated or built from new, live data. And we should track cost and efficiency too, because an agent that needs a thousand steps and a huge budget is a very different thing from one that gets there quickly.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the most useful shift is from asking whether a model gets the right answer on a fixed set of problems to asking what it can do over a longer stretch of work. SWE-bench is valuable, but it's a snapshot: a bounded issue, a known repository, and a test suite that tells you whether the patch passes. Real work involves ambiguous goals, incomplete information, requirements that change midway, and knowing when to stop and ask a question. I'd like to see evaluations that measure how an agent plans, recovers from its own mistakes, and uses tools across hours instead of minutes.

I'd also want evaluations that are harder to game. Once a benchmark becomes the target, people optimize for it, and contamination creeps in. Refreshing tasks regularly and grading outcomes rather than surface patterns helps a lot.

Finally, I think we should look at the process as well as the final result. Two systems can reach the same answer, one through sound reasoning and the other by luck. For anything with real consequences, that difference matters a great deal.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see evaluations move toward tasks that are longer term and more interactive. A benchmark gives you a problem, and you produce an answer or a patch. But in practice, figuring out what the problem is can be a big part of the work. You may need to ask someone a question, explore an unfamiliar environment, or revise your approach when something changes.

So, for a coding agent, I’d be interested in whether it can work with a person to build something over multiple iterations. Can it handle changing requirements? Can it recognize when it’s stuck and recover? And how much human intervention does it need?

I also think we should measure whether an agent gets better with experience. If it makes a mistake on one task, does that experience help it on the next one? That would tell us something beyond whether it can solve a fixed set of problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see evaluations that start with a goal somebody actually cares about, where figuring out what to do is part of the task. Can the system take a somewhat ambiguous request, ask the right questions, and carry it through to a useful result?

And I think the interaction matters. If you’re working with an AI, you might give it feedback halfway through, or change a constraint. Does it adapt? When something goes wrong, can it recognize that and recover? Those are things I’d want an evaluation to capture, alongside whether it ultimately succeeds.

I’d also want to measure how much human help it needed. A system that completes a task with constant supervision is useful in a different way from one you can reliably delegate to. So I’d like evaluations to tell us more about that relationship: what can I hand over, how much attention will it take, and when should the system come back and ask me for help?
